transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in today?

Now that I’m supposed to be slowing down with my partial retirement, I feel like I’m always on the go and can’t just sit still and relax, even for a short visit or a quiet meal. I expected my life to get quieter, but instead, I feel this constant restlessness that I can't seem to shake.
Did this restlessness and inability to relax start after the change to partial retirement, and has it been going on for more than 6 months?

Yes, it became highly noticeable about eight months ago, shortly after I started transitioning into partial retirement. Having less structured days made this lifelong tendency of mine much more obvious, so it has definitely been an ongoing issue for over six months now.
Do you feel this restlessness and worry happen across many areas of life, even when nothing specific is going on, or is it mainly tied to the retirement transition and other recent stressors?

It isn't really anxiety or worry, but more of a physical, pent-up energy that I've actually had my entire life, dating back to primary school when teachers complained I couldn't stay in my seat. The loss of my structured school schedule has just made this lifelong need to be constantly in motion much more obvious and harder to manage.
Did you have these attention, impulsivity, or hyperactivity symptoms clearly before age 12, in more than one setting such as school, home, or work?

Yes, absolutely, these issues go all the way back to my childhood before I was 12. In primary school, my teachers constantly complained to my parents that I couldn't stay in my seat, was always chatting, and would find any excuse to get up and wander around while others worked quietly.

Besides being restless and unable to sit still, do you also have ongoing problems with attention, like losing things, making careless mistakes, or being easily distracted, or with impulsivity, like interrupting others or acting before thinking?

I don't really have those attention issues like losing things or making careless mistakes. But I definitely struggle with impulsivity, like jumping into other people's sentences, finishing my husband's thoughts, and blurting out my ideas before they can even finish.
Do these restlessness and impulsive behaviors still cause problems for you in more than one setting now, such as at home, with friends, or in social activities?

Yes, they definitely cause problems in multiple areas of my life. At home, my husband gets quite irritated because I can't just sit and stay present with him without constantly jumping up to do things. It also makes social activities like my book club or family dinners feel stressful instead of enjoyable, because I just can't relax and keep wanting to get up.
Do you often make impulsive decisions that you later regret, such as spending too much, interrupting others a lot, or acting without thinking?

I don't really struggle with impulsive spending at all. However, I definitely interrupt others a lot, constantly jumping into sentences, finishing my husband's thoughts, or blurting things out in meetings before realizing I've done it, which I always feel bad about afterward.

Do you also have clear problems with inattention, such as being easily distracted, making careless mistakes, losing things, or forgetting tasks, or is it mainly restlessness and impulsive interrupting?

No, I don't really struggle with losing things, making careless mistakes, or forgetting tasks. My difficulties are almost entirely about the physical restlessness, the constant urge to keep moving, and my bad habit of talking too much and interrupting others.

Do these restlessness and impulsive behaviors ever cause you to act in ways that are risky or hard to control, like leaving your seat in situations where you’re expected to stay put, or feeling unable to wait your turn?

Yes, I frequently feel compelled to leave my seat, popping up during book club or family dinners to do unnecessary tasks like clearing plates because sitting still feels unbearable. I also really struggle to wait my turn in conversations, often blurting out my thoughts and interrupting others before they can even finish.

Have these restlessness and impulsive behaviors caused problems at work or in school in the past, such as trouble completing tasks, getting in trouble for talking too much, or being seen as disruptive?

Yes, they definitely did, especially back when I was in school. Even in primary school, my teachers constantly complained to my parents that I couldn't stay in my seat and was always chatting with my classmates. I was always finding excuses to get up, like sharpening my pencil or wandering the room, while everyone else was working quietly.
Did these restlessness and impulsive behaviors continue through adolescence and adulthood, or did they mainly happen only in childhood and then go away?

These behaviors have definitely been lifelong and never really went away during my adulthood. However, the strict structure of my teaching career, with its tight bell schedules and meeting agendas, helped keep me anchored and managed for decades. It is only now, as I'm transitioning into retirement without that constant structure, that it has become highly noticeable and difficult to manage again.
Before age 12, did these behaviors cause problems in more than one setting, such as both at school and at home?

Yes, they did, because my behavior at school directly impacted my home life when teachers constantly complained to my parents. In primary school, they frequently told my parents that I couldn't stay in my seat, was always chatting, and kept popping up to wander around or sharpen my pencil. It was a constant source of discussion and stress at home.
Do you remember having these symptoms before age 12 in more than one setting, such as both at school and at home, or did they start later in life?

Yes, they definitely started before age 12 and were present in both settings. In primary school, my teachers constantly complained to my parents that I couldn't stay in my seat, was always chatting, and kept popping up to wander the room or sharpen my pencil. My parents would then have to address it with me at home, so it was definitely an issue both at school and at home.
Do you also have trouble finishing tasks or staying focused when reading, listening to conversations, or doing paperwork, or is it mostly the restlessness and interrupting?

It is indeed mostly the physical restlessness and interrupting, as I don't really struggle with finishing tasks or focusing on paperwork after managing a long career as a teacher. When I try to read, the issue isn't that I lose focus on the text, but rather that sitting still for that long makes me feel physically agitated and pent-up. I just feel this constant, uncomfortable need to be in motion.
Did you have these symptoms continuously from childhood into adulthood, or were there long periods when they were absent?

They have been continuous since childhood and never actually went away. Back in primary school, teachers always noted I couldn't stay in my seat and chatted constantly, but as an adult, these traits were masked and kept in check by the tight structure of my teaching career. It's only since cutting back on work eight months ago and losing that structure that they have become highly noticeable again.

Have you ever had clear symptoms of inattention as well, such as being easily distracted, making careless mistakes, losing things, or forgetting appointments/tasks, or has it mainly always been restlessness and impulsive interrupting?

It has mainly always been about the physical restlessness, the constant need to be in motion, and my habit of interrupting others. I don't really struggle with losing things, forgetting appointments, or being easily distracted at all. It is definitely the hyperactivity and impulsivity that have always stood out for me throughout my life.
Before age 12, did you also have clear trouble paying attention or being easily distracted, or was it mainly hyperactivity and impulsive behavior like fidgeting, leaving your seat, and interrupting?

It was definitely mainly the hyperactivity and impulsive behaviors rather than any issues with attention. Back in primary school, teachers always told my parents that I could never stay in my seat, was constantly chatting, and would frequently pop up to sharpen my pencil or wander the room while everyone else worked quietly.

Have you ever had clear problems with inattention, such as being easily distracted, making careless mistakes, losing things, or forgetting appointments, or has it mainly always been restlessness and impulsive interrupting?

It has almost entirely been about my physical restlessness, the constant need to be in motion, and my tendency to interrupt. As a teacher, I’ve always been very organized and don't struggle with losing things, forgetting appointments, or making careless mistakes. The real challenge for me has always been my inability to sit still, stay quiet, and relax.

Have you ever had clear problems with inattention, like being easily distracted, making careless mistakes, losing things, or forgetting appointments, or has it mainly always been restlessness and impulsive interrupting?

No, I really don't have those inattention problems like losing things or forgetting appointments at all. My struggles have almost entirely been about my physical restlessness, being constantly in motion, and interrupting others. The real challenge for me is simply the inability to sit still and quiet my mind and body.

Have you ever had clear problems with inattention, such as being easily distracted, making careless mistakes, losing things, or forgetting appointments, or has it mainly always been restlessness and impulsive interrupting?

As I've mentioned, I really don't struggle with inattention, losing things, or forgetting appointments at all. My difficulties have always been entirely about my physical restlessness, being constantly on the go, and blurting things out. Even when I was a child, the feedback was always about my inability to sit still, my constant chatting, and my tendency to interrupt.

opening_question.question: Hello, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has a lifelong history beginning before age 12 of hyperactivity and impulsivity across multiple settings (school and home), with persistent restlessness, inability to remain seated, excessive talking, interrupting/blurting out, and difficulty waiting turn. Symptoms continued into adulthood and cause current impairment in social and home settings. Inattention symptoms are repeatedly denied, making a predominantly hyperactive/impulsive presentation most consistent with F90.1.
